how_to_use: Pick a design, then walk its 12 stages. Each stage has a gate ('done_when') you pass before moving on. Checklist ids are stable (design.stage.nn) so the app can store ticks. Lean designs inherit generic defaults where they have no design-specific text; 'source_of_fields' says which applies.

generic.why: Most wasted research hours start with a question nobody needed answered. An hour of gap-checking saves six months of work on a redundant paper.
generic.what: Turn a clinical itch into one answerable, novel question with a clear population, comparison and outcome.
how: 1. Write the itch down the same day (gap log: one line per idea).
2. Frame it as PICO / PECO / PIRD / PCC in one sentence.
3. Run a 20-minute PubMed search plus PROSPERO, OSF and trial registries for overlap.
4. Score it with FINER (Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant).
5. Check whether it maps to a JLA priority, NICE research recommendation or BOAST.
6. Pick the design that answers it (see design decision tree in Part A §2.2).
7. Name one target journal and its reporting guideline now.
generic.people_needed: You; a 10-minute sense-check with a consultant
pitfalls: Falling for a question that 5 MAs already answered
Choosing a design before the question
templates: One-page idea brief (PICO + FINER + target journal)

generic.why: The design fixes the ceiling on how believable the result can be. The team decides whether it ever gets finished.
generic.what: Lock the design details and assemble a small team with written roles and authorship order.
how: 1. Confirm the design fits the question (intervention -> RCT/cohort; rare outcome -> case-control; test -> DTA).
2. List the people you need: second reviewer/data collector, statistician, senior author.
3. Ask the consultant senior author with a one-page brief and a small, specific ask.
4. Agree authorship order and CRediT roles in writing (ICMJE four criteria).
5. Set WIP limit: is there room in your pipeline (max 4 led by you)?
6. Book a fortnightly 30-minute stand-up.
done_when: Roles and deadlines on the tracker
generic.people_needed: You, consultant senior author, 1-3 juniors (FY/CT/students), statistician contact
pitfalls: Recruiting too many co-authors (BJJ max 8 authors)
Starting work before the consultant is on board

generic.why: Research cannot be approved after the fact. A paper without the right approval can be retracted, and journals increasingly ask for proof.
generic.what: Classify the project (research, service evaluation, audit, or not human research) and obtain the matching approvals.
how: 1. Run the HRA 'Is my study research?' tool; save the PDF.
2. If research: run 'Do I need NHS REC review?'; save the PDF.
3. Email Blackpool R&D (bfwh.researchideas@nhs.net) with the outline and tool outputs.
4. Secure sponsor, GCP (<3 years), DPIA screening and Caldicott advice as needed.
5. Audit/service evaluation: register with the clinical governance/audit team.
6. Do not collect data until the green-light email arrives.
done_when: Approval letter / registration number / 'no approval needed' statement filed
generic.time_estimate: Audit 1-4 weeks; anonymised retrospective research 2-4 months; prospective REC 3-5 months (HRA median 60 days)
generic.people_needed: You, supervisor, R&D, IG/DPO, Caldicott Guardian (if identifiable data)
pitfalls: Researcher outside the care team seeing identifiable notes (CAG needed)
Using personal devices or email for data

generic.why: A dated, public protocol stops you (and reviewers) suspecting you moved the goalposts. Editors now expect it.
generic.what: Write the protocol and statistical analysis plan, then register them publicly before seeing outcome data.
how: 1. Use the design's protocol standard (PRISMA-P, SPIRIT 2025, STROBE headings).
2. Write the SAP: outcomes, models, confounders, missing data, sensitivity analyses.
3. Get statistician and senior author sign-off.
4. Register on PROSPERO (SR), OSF (observational, scoping), ISRCTN/ClinicalTrials.gov (trials).
5. Save protocol v1.0 as PDF with the date; keep an amendments log.

generic.why: Garbage in, garbage out. Errors made here cannot be fixed by clever statistics.
generic.what: Collect the evidence or data exactly as the protocol says, in a structure ready for analysis.
how: 1. Build the data dictionary first (variable, type, codes, source).
2. Pilot the form on 10 cases or the search on known studies.
3. Collect into REDCap or a locked Excel table, one row per patient/record.
4. Log every decision and date.
done_when: Data or search complete and frozen
pitfalls: Free-text fields for things you will analyse
Collecting identifiers you do not need

generic.why: This is where bias creeps in quietly: inconsistent inclusion, duplicates and silent missing data.
generic.what: Apply eligibility criteria consistently and make the dataset analysis-ready, with every change scripted.
how: 1. Run checks in a script (R) not by eye.
2. Report missingness per variable.
3. Keep raw and clean files separate.
pitfalls: Editing the raw file by hand

checklist.text: Cleaning script runs end to end

generic.why: The analysis must answer the registered question, not the most exciting one in the data.
generic.what: Run the pre-specified analysis, then sensitivity analyses, with code a statistician can re-run.
how: 1. Follow the SAP line by line.
2. Report effect sizes with 95% CIs, not just p-values.
3. Run pre-specified sensitivity analyses.
4. List any deviations with reasons.

generic.why: Reviewers read Table 1, the flow diagram and the main figure before the text. Bad figures signal bad science.
generic.what: Make journal-quality tables and figures that tell the story without the text.
how: 1. Flow diagram first (PRISMA/CONSORT/STROBE).
2. Table 1 baseline characteristics.
3. One main figure for the primary outcome.
4. Export at 300+ dpi (TIFF/PDF) or vector.
done_when: Flow diagram, Table 1 and main figure final
pitfalls: Bar charts hiding individual data (BJJ discourages)

generic.why: A clear paper gets reviewed; a muddled one gets desk-rejected, whatever the data.
generic.what: Draft in the fast order: methods, results, tables, discussion, introduction, abstract, title.
how: 1. Paste the reporting checklist into the manuscript as comments.
2. Write methods from the protocol.
3. Write results from the tables.
4. Discussion: main finding, comparison, strengths/limits, implications.
5. Introduction funnel (3 paragraphs).
6. Abstract last; title last.
7. Circulate to co-authors with a 2-week deadline.
done_when: Reporting checklist complete with page numbers
pitfalls: Letting AI write the discussion or references (your rule)
Word limit includes references at BJJ (4,000 words)

generic.why: The wrong journal costs 2-4 months per rejection. The right one is indexed for ST3 and fits the article type.
generic.what: Pick a 3-journal ladder, format for the first, submit cleanly.
how: 1. Check NLM Catalog (MEDLINE) and Clarivate MJL (SCIE/ESCI) on the day.
2. Check article type, word/author limits and preprint policy.
3. Format for journal 1; keep journal 2 version ready.
4. Write a short cover letter: gap, finding, why this journal.
done_when: Tracker updated with next two journals

generic.why: Most accepted papers went through at least one revision. A calm, complete response converts 'major revision' into acceptance.
generic.what: Answer every comment, change the manuscript, and resubmit fast; after rejection, move down the ladder within 14 days.
how: 1. Read the reviews, wait a day, then sort comments into must-fix / can-fix / politely disagree.
2. Build a point-by-point table with line numbers.
3. Re-run analyses if asked; never hide a change.
4. After rejection: fix the fair points and resubmit to journal 2 within 14 days.
generic.people_needed: You + co-authors + statistician for stats comments
pitfalls: Sitting on a rejection for months

generic.why: A paper nobody reads does little for patients or your CV. ST3 evidence also needs to be filed while you remember where it is.
generic.what: Record the output, file the ST3 evidence and turn it into talks.
how: 1. Record PMID, DOI, WoS listing screenshot.
2. Update ORCID, Google Scholar, CV.
3. Save the PDF + acceptance email in the ST3 evidence pack.
4. Submit an abstract to a national/international meeting if not done.
5. Share on X/LinkedIn and with the department.
generic.next: Back to Stage 1: log the next idea from your paper's 'future research' section.
pitfalls: Not checking the paper actually appears in WoS
Presenting the same data twice in one region/season

stages.why: Editors now reject redundant 'me-too' reviews on sight. Your idea only works if no up-to-date, good-quality SR answers it, or yours clearly adds something.
stages.what: A focused review question with a documented overlap check and a written 'why us, why now' rationale.
how: 1. Mine Cochrane 'implications for research', NICE research recommendations (CG124, NG38), JLA PSPs and new BOASTs.
2. Search PubMed with a systematic-review filter, Cochrane Library, PROSPERO, Epistemonikos and OSF for existing or in-progress reviews.
3. If an SR exists: check its date, AMSTAR 2 quality, and whether 2+ sizeable RCTs have appeared since.
4. Check ClinicalTrials.gov/ISRCTN: is a big trial about to report? If so, wait or plan a living review.
5. Run a rough PubMed search: under 3 eligible studies = no meta-analysis; over ~80 = narrow it.
6. Write the PICO(S) with the primary outcome AND its time point.
7. Draft the rationale paragraph that names prior reviews and your added value (PRISMA item 3).
done_when: Overlap check saved with date and screenshots
PICO frozen with primary outcome + time point
stages.people_needed: You + consultant senior author (10-minute sense check)
pitfalls: Topic already covered by a 2-year-old high-quality MA
Ignoring PROSPERO records still in progress
Topic outside your specialty (an SR-mill signature)
Question too broad for a team of 3

examples.how_they_did_it: Justified a new MA because the large HEALTH trial had reported since the last reviews; the update changed the weight of evidence.
examples.paper: Total Hip Arthroplasty Versus Hemiarthroplasty for Displaced Femoral Neck Fracture: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

examples.how_they_did_it: Took a heavily reviewed topic (distal radius fixation) and added value by focusing on age as an effect modifier.
examples.paper: Operative management of displaced fractures of the distal radius is associated with improved function but not in older adults: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

numbers.how_they_did_it: Around 682 SRs entered MEDLINE in one month in 2014, so overlap is the norm, not the exception.
numbers.paper: Page MJ, Shamseer L, Altman DG, Tetzlaff J, Sampson M, Tricco AC, et al. Epidemiology and reporting characteristics of systematic reviews of biomedical research: a cross-sectional study. PLoS Med. 2016;13(5):e1002028.

numbers.fact: Rule of thumb: fewer than 3 comparable studies means no pooling; more than about 80 means split or narrow.

checklist.text: PICO + primary outcome + time point frozen

stages.why: Two independent reviewers are not optional. A review run by one person will be rejected, and a review run by too many unclear people looks like a paper mill.
stages.what: Choose the review type and recruit the minimum viable team with written roles.
how: 1. Pick the type: pairwise SR+MA, SR without MA (SWiM), NMA, DTA, MA of proportions, scoping, umbrella (see Part B §1.4).
2. Recruit Reviewer 2 (FY/CT/student) for independent screening, extraction and risk of bias.
3. Name Reviewer 3 as arbiter (registrar/fellow).
4. Ask the Trust librarian to build or peer-review the search (credit them).
5. Find a statistician if pooling (essential for NMA or DTA).
6. Sign the authorship agreement: order, CRediT roles, 'silence after 3 weeks = approval'.
7. Give each reviewer a 1-hour onboarding (Cochrane Interactive Learning modules).
stages.people_needed: You (lead), Reviewer 2, arbiter, librarian, statistician, consultant
pitfalls: Second reviewer who drops out mid-screening (recruit a reserve)
More than 8 authors if targeting BJJ

examples.how_they_did_it: Published SRs averaged a team of 5 people; funded reviews used about 7. Plan for 4-5.
examples.paper: Borah R, Brown AW, Capers PL, Kaiser KA. Analysis of the time and workers needed to conduct systematic reviews of medical interventions using data from the PROSPERO registry. BMJ Open. 2017;7(2):e012545.

numbers.fact: Mean team size 5 (SD 3) for published SRs.
numbers.source: Borah R, Brown AW, Capers PL, Kaiser KA. Analysis of the time and workers needed to conduct systematic reviews of medical interventions using data from the PROSPERO registry. BMJ Open. 2017;7(2):e012545.

templates: Role cards (lead, reviewer 2, arbiter, librarian, statistician, senior)

stages.why: SRs use published data, so they do not need ethics approval. Saying so clearly in the paper avoids an editor query.
stages.what: Confirm and document that no ethics approval is needed; registration replaces it.
how: 1. Note in the protocol: 'Ethics approval not required; analysis of published data.'
2. If you will obtain unpublished individual patient data from authors, check with R&D or the university.
3. Move straight to protocol and PROSPERO registration.
tools: HRA decision tool (optional, for the file)
pitfalls: Asking authors for patient-level data without a data-sharing agreement

examples.how_they_did_it: 27-item checklist plus flow diagram; the yardstick every SR is judged against.
examples.paper: Page MJ et al. The PRISMA 2020 statement. BMJ 2021;372:n71

stages.why: Registration before screening is the single best signal of honesty in a review. PROSPERO refuses reviews with extraction already done.
stages.what: A PRISMA-P protocol (17 items) and a PROSPERO record (or OSF for scoping reviews).
how: 1. Write a 4-8 page protocol using PRISMA-P headings.
2. Include the full draft MEDLINE strategy as an appendix.
3. Specify RoB tool per design (RoB 2, ROBINS-I V2, QUADAS-2).
4. Specify synthesis: effect measure, REML + Hartung-Knapp, subgroups with expected direction, sensitivity analyses, GRADE.
5. Submit to PROSPERO (2025 system, automatic duplicate check); state the stage honestly.
6. Start the search once submitted; do not wait for the CRD number.
7. Optional: publish the protocol (BMJ Open, Systematic Reviews) only for NMA/IPD-scale work.
pitfalls: Relying only on paid registries such as INPLASY

examples.how_they_did_it: Cochrane reviews publish a full protocol first; deviations are listed in the final review. Copy that habit.
examples.paper: Interventions for treating proximal humeral fractures in adults

numbers.fact: PROSPERO registration now typically takes 1-4 weeks after the 2025 rebuild.

stages.why: A PubMed-only search is one of the top reasons SRs are rejected. Search quality decides whether you missed the trial that changes the answer.
stages.what: A peer-reviewed, reproducible multi-database search with deduplicated exports.
how: 1. Split PICO into concepts (usually P + I + design filter; avoid searching outcomes).
2. Build MeSH + free text for MEDLINE; rebuild with Emtree for Embase (they differ).
3. Use validated filters: Cochrane HSSS for RCTs; SIGN/ISSG filters for others.
4. Test against 5-10 known eligible studies: all must appear.
5. Peer-review with PRESS 2015 (librarian or second searcher).
6. Run MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, WoS/Scopus (+ CINAHL if rehab) within 1-2 days; add ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP.
7. Export RIS with abstracts; deduplicate (EndNote Bramer method, Rayyan, Deduklick) and log counts.
8. Plan forward/backward citation chasing (CitationChaser).
done_when: Raw exports + dedup log + exact dates saved
Full strategies ready for the supplement
pitfalls: Not recording search dates and platforms
Search older than 6-12 months at submission (re-run it)

examples.how_they_did_it: Searched specialised trauma registers, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase and trial registries, with full strategies in appendices.
examples.paper: Interventions for treating proximal humeral fractures in adults

numbers.fact: Initial search hits ranged from 27 to 92,020 records across published SRs.
numbers.source: Borah R, Brown AW, Capers PL, Kaiser KA. Analysis of the time and workers needed to conduct systematic reviews of medical interventions using data from the PROSPERO registry. BMJ Open. 2017;7(2):e012545.

numbers.fact: Typical orthopaedic intervention SR: 1,000-5,000 records after deduplication.

stages.why: Single-reviewer screening misses eligible studies. Reviewers check that your flow numbers add up; mismatches are a classic catch.
stages.what: Independent dual screening at title/abstract and full text, with agreement statistics and reasons for exclusion.
how: 1. Pilot on 50-100 records together; refine criteria until agreement is about 90%.
2. Screen titles/abstracts independently in blind mode (Rayyan/Covidence); include if in doubt.
3. Retrieve full texts; screen independently; record one main reason per exclusion (design > population > intervention > comparator > outcome > duplicate dataset).
4. Resolve conflicts by discussion, then the arbiter.
5. Calculate Cohen's kappa at each stage (irr::kappa2).
6. Link multiple reports of the same study; pick the most complete report per outcome.
7. If using AI prioritisation (ASReview), report the tool, version and stopping rule; never use an LLM as the only second reviewer.
pitfalls: Double counting overlapping cohorts or registry reports
Reviewer 2 seeing your decisions (blind mode off)
No reasons recorded for full-text exclusions

examples.how_they_did_it: 27-item checklist plus flow diagram; the yardstick every SR is judged against.
examples.paper: Page MJ et al. The PRISMA 2020 statement. BMJ 2021;372:n71

numbers.fact: Median 63 full texts screened per published SR (maximum 4,385); about 3% of retrieved records end up included.
numbers.source: Borah R, Brown AW, Capers PL, Kaiser KA. Analysis of the time and workers needed to conduct systematic reviews of medical interventions using data from the PROSPERO registry. BMJ Open. 2017;7(2):e012545.

numbers.fact: Kappa 0.61-0.80 = substantial, >0.80 = almost perfect agreement.

stages.why: Extraction errors (SE taken as SD, wrong arm) are common and change results. Risk of bias that never affects the synthesis is a classic reviewer complaint.
stages.what: Double extraction with a piloted form, design-appropriate risk of bias, and a synthesis that uses the RoB results.
how: 1. Pilot the extraction form on 2-3 studies with Reviewer 2; revise.
2. Double-extract outcome data independently; verify all other fields.
3. Pre-define time-point windows and an outcome hierarchy (e.g. PRWE > DASH > QuickDASH).
4. Convert medians/IQR with Luo (mean) and Wan/Shi (SD); flag every conversion.
5. Digitise graph-only data with WebPlotDigitizer; email authors twice, 2 weeks apart, for missing data.
6. Assess RoB in duplicate: RoB 2 (RCTs), ROBINS-I V2 (non-randomised), QUADAS-2 (DTA).
7. Synthesise (narrative/SWiM if no pooling; see meta_analysis for pooling) and grade certainty with GRADE.
tools: Excel/Google Sheets or SRDR+ or Covidence
pitfalls: Mixing change scores and final values with SMD
Summing RoB into a single score

examples.how_they_did_it: Used GRADE Summary of Findings tables so every conclusion carries a certainty rating.
examples.paper: Interventions for treating proximal humeral fractures in adults

numbers.fact: SD = SE x sqrt(n); SE from a 95% CI = (upper - lower) / 3.92 (large samples).

stages.why: Reviewers open the PRISMA flow, the characteristics table and the RoB figure first.
stages.what: PRISMA 2020 flow diagram, study characteristics table, RoB traffic-light plot, forest plot(s) and Summary of Findings table.
how: 1. Make the flow diagram with the PRISMA2020 app; check every number reconciles.
2. Characteristics table: study, country, design, n, population, intervention, comparator, follow-up.
3. RoB traffic light + summary bar plot with robvis.
4. Summary of Findings table from GRADEpro with absolute effects per 1,000.
5. Move everything else to the supplement.
done_when: Flow, characteristics, RoB figure and SoF table final
pitfalls: Flow diagram numbers that do not add up

examples.how_they_did_it: 27-item checklist plus flow diagram; the yardstick every SR is judged against.
examples.paper: Page MJ et al. The PRISMA 2020 statement. BMJ 2021;372:n71

stages.why: SR papers live or die on transparency. Missing PRISMA items are easy desk-rejection reasons.
stages.what: A 3,500-4,500 word manuscript mirroring the protocol, with conclusions in GRADE language.
how: 1. Paste PRISMA 2020 items into the draft as comments.
2. Methods mirror the protocol and cite Handbook v6.5, RoB 2, GRADE.
3. Results: flow -> characteristics -> RoB -> primary synthesis -> sensitivity -> reporting bias -> certainty.
4. Discussion: main finding in GRADE words ('probably reduces' = moderate), comparison with prior SRs, limits of the evidence and of the review, the exact trial needed next.
5. Abstract: registration ID, search date, studies/participants, effect + CI, I2/prediction interval, certainty.
6. Add data/code availability (OSF/GitHub DOI) and an AI-use statement if relevant.
done_when: PRISMA 2020 + abstract checklist with page numbers
pitfalls: Spin: strong recommendations from low-certainty evidence
Not explaining why your result differs from previous MAs

examples.how_they_did_it: Abstract states the number of RCTs and patients, the pooled effects, and frames results against the new trial evidence.
examples.paper: Total Hip Arthroplasty Versus Hemiarthroplasty for Displaced Femoral Neck Fracture: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

numbers.fact: Target 3,500-4,500 words; BJJ caps all articles at 4,000 words including abstract and references.

stages.why: SR-friendly, ST3-eligible journals differ a lot in appetite and cost.
stages.what: A three-step ladder of MEDLINE + SCIE journals that publish SRs.
how: 1. Ladder example: EFORT Open Reviews -> JBJS Reviews -> Bone & Joint Open -> BMC MSK / JOSR.
2. For trauma topics: Injury or AOTS.
3. Check BJJ's preprint ban if you posted on medRxiv.
4. Upload PRISMA checklist, PROSPERO ID, search strategies and data/code links.
pitfalls: Paying APCs at a hybrid journal when the free route exists

stages.why: Common SR reviewer requests are predictable: updated search, sensitivity analyses, GRADE, overlap with prior reviews.
stages.what: A point-by-point response and, if needed, a search update.
how: 1. If more than 6 months since search, re-run it before responding.
2. Add requested sensitivity analyses; report even if results do not change.
3. Explain discordance with other MAs calmly with a table.
done_when: Response sent or cascaded within 14 days
pitfalls: Refusing to update an old search

numbers.fact: BJJ first decision 6-8 weeks; realistic total to acceptance 4-9 months.

stages.why: SRs are cited heavily if people know they exist. They also convert well into podium talks.
stages.what: Close the PROSPERO record, file evidence, present it.
how: 1. Update the PROSPERO record to 'completed' with the publication link.
2. Submit to EFORT, BOA or the subspecialty society.
3. Note the 'implications for research' as the next project's idea.
stages.next: Back to Stage 1: log the next idea from your paper's 'future research' section.

examples.how_they_did_it: Only about 24% of UK orthopaedic meeting abstracts become papers. Doing it the other way round (paper first) beats the odds.
examples.paper: Analysis of conference abstract-to-publication rate in UK orthopaedic meetings (see KB E_sources S12).

meta_analysis.label: Meta-analysis (pairwise / NMA / proportions)
meta_analysis.st3: Counts as part of the SR paper.
meta_analysis.note: Use together with systematic_review: this track covers what pooling adds at each stage.

stages.why: A meta-analysis only makes sense when studies are similar enough to combine. Pooling apples and oranges is a top rejection reason.
stages.what: Confirm that at least 3 comparable studies report the same outcome in a poolable form.
how: 1. Scan the likely included studies: same comparison, similar population, same outcome at similar time point?
2. Decide the effect measure up front (RR, MD, SMD, HR, proportion).
3. If studies differ fundamentally, plan a SWiM narrative synthesis instead.
4. If 3+ treatments compete, consider NMA (needs a statistician).
stages.time_estimate: Within the SR idea stage (1-2 weeks)
pitfalls: Planning to pool RCTs with non-randomised studies
Meta-analysis of 2 small trials with strong conclusions

examples.how_they_did_it: Pooled only RCTs comparing THA with hemiarthroplasty for displaced femoral neck fractures.
examples.paper: Total Hip Arthroplasty Versus Hemiarthroplasty for Displaced Femoral Neck Fracture: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

numbers.fact: Funnel plots and Egger tests need at least 10 studies; meta-regression needs about 10 studies per covariate.
numbers.source: Cochrane Handbook v6.5 / KB Part B §7.3-7.5

stages.why: Statistical mistakes in MAs are common and easy for reviewers to spot.
stages.what: Add a statistician or methodologist to the SR team before analysis.
how: 1. Share the protocol synthesis section with the statistician early.
2. Agree software (R meta/metafor) and who writes and checks code.
done_when: Statistician named as co-author with CRediT role
pitfalls: Statistician brought in only to 'check' finished results

stages.why: Same as the parent SR: no ethics for published data.
stages.what: Document no ethics needed.
how: 1. Copy the SR statement.

stages.why: Pre-specified models and subgroups stop you choosing the analysis that gives the nicest p-value.
stages.what: A synthesis plan inside the PROSPERO record and protocol.
how: 1. Specify random-effects with REML tau2 and Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman CIs (Cochrane default since RevMan update).
2. Name subgroups with the expected direction of effect, and why.
3. List sensitivity analyses: high-RoB excluded, converted data excluded, common-effect, leave-one-out.
4. Plan zero-cell handling (MH without correction or GLMM) and proportion pooling (GLMM logit, not Freeman-Tukey).
5. Plan reporting-bias assessment only if 10+ studies.
done_when: Synthesis plan in protocol and registry

examples.how_they_did_it: Cochrane moved RevMan to REML and Hartung-Knapp by default; cite this when reviewers ask why.
examples.paper: Cochrane Methods: new random-effects methods in RevMan

stages.why: Identical to the SR search; an incomplete search biases the pooled estimate.
stages.what: See systematic_review stage 5.
how: 1. Follow the SR search steps; search trial registries for unpublished results (reporting-bias check).

stages.why: Duplicate patient data inflates precision.
stages.what: See systematic_review stage 6, plus a unit-of-analysis plan.
how: 1. Link overlapping reports; decide which report feeds each outcome.
2. Write the unit-of-analysis plan: bilateral cases, multi-arm trials (split shared control), cluster trials (design effect).
done_when: One data source per study per outcome
pitfalls: Counting the control arm twice in multi-arm trials

stages.why: The pooled number is what people will quote. It must come from the right model and honest uncertainty.
stages.what: Pool with pre-specified methods; quantify and explore heterogeneity; test robustness.
how: 1. Extract events/totals (binary), mean/SD/n (continuous) or log HR + SE (time-to-event).
2. Run metabin/metacont/metagen with method.tau='REML' and method.random.ci='HK'; show the prediction interval.
3. Report tau2, I2 with its CI and the prediction interval; do not lean on I2 alone.
4. Run pre-specified subgroups and meta-regression (about 10 studies per covariate); judge credibility with ICEMAN.
5. Run sensitivity analyses (leave-one-out, high-RoB removed, conversions removed).
6. Small-study effects: funnel + Egger/Harbord/Peters only if 10+ studies; trim-and-fill as sensitivity only.
7. Proportions: metaprop with method='GLMM', sm='PLOGIT'.
8. GRADE each outcome; imprecision judged against the MCID.
9. Archive code and data on OSF/GitHub with a DOI.
done_when: Primary pooled estimate with CI and PI

examples.how_they_did_it: Reported pooled risk ratios for complications and dislocation separately, with heterogeneity statistics.
examples.paper: Total Hip Arthroplasty Versus Hemiarthroplasty for Displaced Femoral Neck Fracture: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

examples.how_they_did_it: Worked R code for every model listed here.
examples.paper: Harrer M et al. Doing Meta-Analysis with R (free online book)

numbers.fact: PRWE MCID about 11-14 points; OKS about 5 points. Use these to judge imprecision.

stages.why: The forest plot is the paper. People screenshot it for teaching.
stages.what: Forest plot per key outcome, funnel plot if 10+ studies, SoF table.
how: 1. Forest: study labels, events/n or mean/SD per arm, weights, pooled diamond, prediction interval, labels saying which side favours which treatment.
2. Sort by effect size or year consistently.
3. Contour-enhanced funnel if 10+ studies.
4. NMA: network graph, league table.

stages.why: Same as SR; add statistical transparency.
stages.what: See systematic_review stage 9, plus full statistical methods.
how: 1. State model, tau2 estimator, CI method, software and version; cite R packages.
done_when: Stats methods paragraph approved by statistician

stages.why: See SR.
stages.what: See SR ladder.
how: 1. Use the SR ladder; NMA suits JBJS Reviews, BJJ, Injury.

stages.why: Statistical reviewers ask for model changes.
stages.what: Run requested re-analyses transparently.
how: 1. Report requested alternative models as sensitivity analyses, not replacements, unless genuinely better.

stages.why: Retrospective cohorts are fast because the data already exist. That same speed tempts people into fishing trips. A sharp question keeps it publishable.

6. Search PubMed for the 3 closest papers; your angle is bigger, UK-specific, better adjusted, or a new outcome.

how: 1. Write protocol using the skeleton in Part A §4.4.
2. SAP: primary model (e.g. logistic or Cox), confounders from DAG, missing data (multiple imputation), sensitivity analyses (complete case, E-value).
3. Register on OSF with the secondary data template; note what data you have already seen (honestly).
4. Statistician signs off the SAP.

stages.why: Most retrospective cohort errors come from inconsistent extraction by different people.
stages.what: A piloted REDCap form or locked Excel table, filled consistently from defined sources.
how: 1. Write the data dictionary: variable, definition, source, allowed values.
2. Build REDCap (preferred) or Excel table with data validation drop-downs.
3. Pilot on 10 records with two collectors; compare; fix definitions.
4. Collect only what the SAP needs (data minimisation).
5. Re-extract a random 10% by a second person; report agreement.
6. Store on the Trust network or REDCap only.

stages.why: Cleaning by hand leaves no audit trail and hides errors. A script makes every change visible and repeatable.
stages.what: A cleaning script that turns raw export into an analysis file, plus a missingness report.
how: 1. Import raw data untouched (readxl/janitor::clean_names).
2. Check structure, types and ranges; flag impossible values (age 210, LOS -3).
3. Recode categories consistently (Male/M/m -> male).
4. Check duplicates by ID.
5. Tabulate missingness per variable (naniar); decide on multiple imputation (mice) if MAR plausible.
6. Produce the STROBE patient flow (eligible -> excluded with reasons -> analysed).
tools: R: tidyverse, janitor, naniar, skimr, mice

stages.why: Reviewers will ask: did you adjust for the right things, and could unmeasured confounding explain it?
stages.what: Pre-specified adjusted model, with effect sizes, CIs and sensitivity analyses.
how: 1. Table 1 by exposure group (gtsummary).
2. Primary model per SAP: logistic (OR) or modified Poisson (RR) for binary; Cox for time-to-event; competing risks (Fine-Gray) if death competes.
3. Check assumptions: linearity (splines), proportional hazards, EPV.
4. Consider propensity score methods (IPTW/matching with cobalt balance checks).
5. Multiple imputation (mice) with outcome in the imputation model; complete case as sensitivity.
6. E-value for unmeasured confounding.
7. Account for clustering by surgeon/hospital if relevant.
tools: R: gtsummary, finalfit, survival, ggsurvfit, tidycmprsk, MatchIt, WeightIt, cobalt, EValue, mice
pitfalls: Kaplan-Meier for revision when death is common (overestimates)

3. Check if a validated questionnaire exists before writing your own.

stages.why: Pilot testing catches confusing questions before they cost you responses.
stages.what: Pilot, launch, remind, close.
how: 1. Pilot with 5-10 people from the target group; time it; fix wording.
2. Launch with a personal cover message from a respected senior.
3. Send 2 reminders; regional leads chase locally.
4. Track responses against the denominator weekly.
5. Close on a fixed date.

stages.why: Your distal radius audit and VTE service evaluation are already half a paper. Journals reject single-cycle audits, so the idea is to close the loop with a real change.
stages.what: A measurable gap against a standard, and a change idea you can test.
how: 1. Pick a standard with a target (BOAST, NICE NG38, local guideline).
2. Write the aim in SMART form: 'Increase X from 55% to 90% by June 2027'.
3. Map the process (fishbone/driver diagram) to find why care falls short.
4. Choose change ideas you can test quickly (proforma, teaching, pathway, IT prompt).
pitfalls: Change idea not under your control

2. Record which change happened when (annotate).
3. Use a simple data form; one row per patient.

how: 1. Start from a teaching problem you own (simulation, fracture clinic teaching, on-call handover).

3. Choose the Kirkpatrick level you can reach: knowledge test, skills score (OSATS), behaviour in theatre.
4. Search Medical Education, Medical Teacher, J Surg Educ for prior work.

2. Use validated assessment (OSATS, global rating scales) with blinded raters.
3. Recruit a co-author with qualitative experience if mixed methods.
4. Agree authorship.
